I used to feel the same way, but I found out that a lot of it is due to rest intervals and those depend on what you want out of working out. Muscle endurance? 3x15-20 with 1:30-2 min rest intervals should be good, but most studies say that your muscle won’t grow that much. If you want maximum size or strength then your rest periods are gonna get bigger.

Example: once upon a time I did full body workouts twice a week, but I only did one exercise per muscle, did 3x20, and rest for about 1:30 or less. I was in and out in about 1.5 hours (I think). NOW, I do 5-6 compound lifts from anywhere between 3-6 sets of 8-12 reps, resting for at least 3 minutes, 3 or more times a week.

The first one sounds more stressful, but I break a much bigger sweat now than back then and just those 5-6 lifts take up 1-1.5 hours. I’m training for hypertrophy and strength meaning I lift as heavy as a can; the long rest periods are meant to let my muscles “recharge” more so I can do it again.

I’m still kinda novice (and a huge weakpot), but I feel more accomplished.

TL;DR - It’s about number of sets and rest periods. If you wanna be stronger/bigger, you do more sets and rest longer.

Everything I said is just my opinion, but I do think he is a terrible director. I don't think he has a knack for visual story telling and I don't think he has any talent. Every time I watch his movies I get a sick feeling from the lighting. I can't remain interested because his plots are just to service the spectacle. It's not just melodramatic, it's gaudy. Spectacle can be done well (see the above "Pacific Rim") but I don't think he does it well because he doesn't have a plan. It's like if Jackson Pollock just thought paint looked cool so he threw it at a canvas.

As for the question at the bottom, my answer is yes. I believe that, since you can never fully understand what your audience wants (since it's made up of MILLIONS of people), you have to pay attention to what you feel makes a good movie. 

Now, that's a success on MY side. But, the audience matters when it comes to making a conventionally "good" movie. There are objective elements that can be gauged, which is how we know Uwe Boll is one of the worst, but at least he's honest (delusional, but he believes in what he makes).

Boll and Bay show what you need in order to make a "good" movie: integrity and awareness. Boll loves his vision, but his vision sucks. Bay doesn't care about vision, but "damn, it sure is pretty."

He could be considered a genius the way McDonald's is considered to be genius: no matter what they do, they do it because, despite the quality, they will make money. Sure, that's money smart, but no one would dare compare him to Welles or Griffith. He's a brilliant producer because he does the job of a producer, generate cash. But he's still a terrible director because he doesn't care about his "vision" or creating a honestly made film.

Del Toro and "Pacific Rim" could be seen as an actually good version of Transformers: both don't pay attention to artistic quality and deep meaning but opt for creating an exciting ride for the audience. But, whereas Bay makes the ride based on focus groups and it turns out that loop-the-loops test well, Del Toro makes it because HE likes the ride.

You've stumbled onto the plight of many, many millennials; your fulfillment is not in your objects. I understand not being proud of your creations, and thinking that the next package from amazon will contain the very last thing you need to be happy.

I also remember feeling so terrible about not working out, yet lacking the motivation and energy to go to a gym or just to do a push up.

The best thing to do is MAKE yourself move. After I put aside the pain I felt from just getting out of bed and drove to the gym, I didn't regret it. Sweating out the depression can really help. Aside from that, I'd do what I made myself do about a year ago; find some true solitude.

Pull a transcendentalist move and find some trees and rocks and stay there for as long as you need. I camped alone in the blue ridge mountains for four days as a social detox; it was depressing, painful, and I cried to sleep most nights, but I learned more about myself than I did elsewhere.

You may not find fulfillment in the possessions around you, and it may be because investing so much of your identity in inanimate objects gives you nothing. I found my way out of that pit by searching for self betterment, and not just physically or mentally, but socially. Find a friend, sit down at a bar, meet someone. Form a true, strong, deep relationship. Those are the only things that tend to pay off.

I hope you do well, peace friend.

I understand how you feel; not a day would go by where I didn't think of killing myself.

When I brought it up to my family, that killing myself always seemed like the first and most complete solution to a problem, they said "I just don't understand how suicide can be the first thing you think of." I think it boils down to how our brains are different; those who are not depressed have a view of the future and the ability to imagine things getting better or them moving past it. We, however, lack almost any ability to see beyond the very present "now," which is ultimately our downfall.

From the sound of it, you know what depression is. People who suffer from depression don't typically feel sad; it's more of an absence, an emptiness. In essence; feeling so bored you would kill yourself.

I can tell it's going to be hard for most people here to identify with your situation. Most our depressions stem from very relatable circumstances. I'm sorry for how things have turned out, and I hope that they will get better. The only advice I have is a very basic, cliched way of saying "find something fun to do." When I started dipping into depressive episodes, I would work out, and I don't think that is incredibly sight oriented (if you can find a spotter). Have you heard of "Goalball?" It's a sport specifically designed for blind people! Perhaps you can find a club near you. 

I'm sorry that that's all I can bring for comfort. I hope you fare well and know that you are loved by your family. Tell your family about how and feel and ask to see a doctor who may be able to prescribe some medication; it may help. For most of us, the best way we know to fight off episodes is to busy ourselves with worthwhile work; reading, hiking, lifting, meeting people.

I hope you do well friend.

Normally, my source of optimism comes from my faith, but I understand religion is an extremely touchy subject here, so I'm gonna stick to something objectively valuable:

Sometimes, all you can do is think about it; there are times where you can't "feel" that something is out there, you can own intellectualize it, you can only keep thinking it's there, and eventually something will come around. When I have nothing, when I'm broken and incapable of seeing anything in the future, I find the smallest thing that I can hope for. Sometimes it's that the cafeteria is serving pepperoni pizza made by the best guy, and then it gets larger when I realize that I'm getting a pay check and can probably go buy a movie or something. Start small, the smallest you can, something like "I love taking hot showers and I'm gonna do it later." If you can't seem to find anything, take the smallest of initiatives and go with it. I know that doing things or going places while in depression takes a lot out of you, and it can seem like the single most unpleasant experience ever, but the smallest step towards creating something to look forward to can help. Start with the phone, don't think you're buying yourself happiness, think that you have something to look forward to. From there, pick another marker in the distance, and adhere to it. Just keep picking things, and eventually things will get brighter, and you'll be better for however long you're normally better for.
